summary: On His way to heal Jairus’s dying daughter, Jesus stops for a woman who touched His garment, then raises the girl from the dead.
key_insight: While Jesus stopped for the woman, Jairus’s daughter died, and the delay looked costly. Yet the woman, unclean for twelve years, became the only person in the Gospels Jesus addresses as “Daughter,” and then He raised Jairus’s twelve-year-old daughter too.
story: When Jesus crossed back over the lake, the crowd welcomed Him, for they had all been waiting for Him. {Lk} One of the rulers of the synagogue, a man named Jairus, came and fell at His feet. {Mk} He had an only daughter, about twelve years old, and she was dying. {Lk} He begged Jesus earnestly, “My little daughter lies at the point of death. Come and lay Your hands on her, that she may be healed, and she will live.” {Mk} So Jesus went with him, and the crowd followed, pressing in on every side.

In that crowd was a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years. She had suffered many things from many physicians and spent all she had, and instead of getting better she grew worse. She had heard about Jesus, and she said, “If only I may touch His clothes, I shall be made well.” {Mk} She came up behind Him and touched the border of His garment. {Lk} Immediately the bleeding stopped, and she felt in her body that she was healed. {Mk}

Jesus knew at once that power had gone out of Him. He turned around in the crowd and said, “Who touched My clothes?” {Mk} When everyone denied it, Peter said, “Master, the multitudes throng and press You, and You say, ‘Who touched Me?’ ” {Lk} But Jesus kept looking around to see who had done it. {Mk} Trembling, the woman came and fell down before Him, and in front of all the people she told why she had touched Him and how she had been healed at once. {Lk} He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be healed of your affliction.” {Mk}

While He was still speaking, messengers came from Jairus’s house: “Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?” Jesus heard it and said to Jairus, “Do not be afraid; only believe.” Then He let no one follow Him except Peter, James and John. {Mk}

At the house, flute players and a noisy crowd were wailing. {Mt} Jesus said, “Why make this commotion and weep? The child is not dead, but sleeping.” {Mk} They ridiculed Him, knowing that she was dead. {Lk} He put them all outside, took the father and mother and His three disciples, and went in where the child lay. {Mk}

He took her by the hand and said, “Talitha, cumi,” which is translated, “Little girl, I say to you, arise.” {Mk} Her spirit returned, {Lk} and immediately she got up and walked. Her parents were overcome with amazement. Jesus commanded them strictly that no one should know it, and told them to give her something to eat. {Mk} Even so, the report went out into all that land. {Mt}
differences: In Matthew the ruler says at the start, “My daughter has just died.” In Mark and Luke she is dying, and messengers bring word of her death later.
Only Mark and Luke name Jairus, record Jesus’ question “Who touched Me?” and tell of the woman’s public confession.
Mark says the woman grew worse under many physicians; Luke says she “could not be healed by any.” Only Matthew mentions the flute players.
Only Mark gives Jesus’ Aramaic words, “Talitha, cumi.” Only Luke says “her spirit returned.”
Matthew says the ruler came while Jesus was speaking about fasting (Matthew 9:14–18); Mark and Luke place his request right after Jesus returned from the country of the Gadarenes.

fit.question: In Matthew, the ruler says his daughter “has just died.” In Mark and Luke, he says she is dying, and only later do messengers report her death. Which is right?

points.label: Matthew tells it short
points.text: Matthew tells both miracles in nine verses, where Mark takes twenty-three. He leaves out the messengers and folds the outcome, the girl’s death, into the father’s first request.

points.label: A father’s fear
points.text: Jairus left her at the point of death. By the time he found Jesus he may well have feared she was already gone, and Matthew gives his plea in its strongest form.

fit.note: Summarizing a story is not getting it wrong; all three agree that the girl died and that Jesus raised her.
fit.short: Matthew compresses the story, leaving out the messengers and putting the girl’s death into the father’s first words.

fit.question: Matthew says the ruler came “while He spoke these things,” that is, while Jesus was answering a question about fasting. Mark and Luke tell the fasting question much earlier. When did Jairus come?

points.label: The same day
points.text: McGarvey held that the meal and the question about fasting took place in Capernaum on the day Jesus returned across the lake, so Jairus came while Jesus was still at the table. Mark and Luke tell the fasting question earlier in their books, grouped with other conflict stories.

points.label: Grouped by theme
points.text: Others think one of the writers arranged these stories by subject rather than by date, and that Matthew’s link is looser than it first sounds.

fit.note: The Gospel writers often group stories by subject, and the text does not settle which order is by date.
fit.short: Either the fasting question came the same day Jesus returned across the lake, or the writers grouped these stories by theme.

scene.label: Ruler of the synagogue
scene.text: A synagogue ruler was a respected lay leader who arranged the Sabbath services and chose who would read and speak (Acts 13:15). For such a man to fall at Jesus’ feet in public was no small thing.

scene.label: Twelve years unclean
scene.text: Under the Law, a woman with a constant flow of blood was unclean, and so was anything she touched (Leviticus 15:25–27). For twelve years she had been kept at a distance from worship and from ordinary touch.

scene.label: The border of His garment
scene.text: Jewish men wore tassels on the corners of their outer garment, as God had commanded (Numbers 15:38–39). The “border” she touched was probably one of these.

scene.label: Flutes and mourners
scene.text: Mourning began as soon as someone died. A Jewish writing from about AD 200 says even the poorest husband should hire at least two flute players and one wailing woman for his wife’s funeral. The crowd at Jairus’s house was already in full grief.

witnesses.matthew: Tells both miracles in nine verses, the briefest account. In his chain of ten miracles (chapters 8–9), this one shows the King’s power reaching even death, and Matthew notes that the report spread “into all that land.”
witnesses.mark: Gives the fullest telling and places the woman’s story inside Jairus’s, a pattern Mark often uses. He alone keeps Jesus’ Aramaic words and notes that the girl got up and walked, the kind of detail Peter, who was in the room, would remember.
witnesses.luke: Notes that she was an only daughter, that her spirit returned, and that the woman told her story “in the presence of all the people.” Luke shows Jesus restoring an outsider in public and giving her a place of honor.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is Lord over twelve years of sickness no doctor could cure, and over death itself. He calls death sleep, because for Him raising the dead is as simple as waking a child.
seeing.living: Jesus would not let the woman slip away healed but unseen; He called her out to give her a word: “Daughter.” And when the worst news reached Jairus, Jesus spoke before fear could: “Do not be afraid; only believe.” When Jesus seems to be busy with someone else and your news gets worse, keep walking with Him to the house.
seeing.ponder: When bad news comes and others say, “Why trouble the Teacher any further?”, what keeps you walking with Jesus?

preaching.big_idea: No one is too unclean to touch Jesus, and nothing is too late for Him.
outline: A hidden woman made a daughter (25–34)
A word for the worst news (35–36)
preaching.watch_for: Mark places the woman’s story inside Jairus’s. The two belong together: twelve years, a “daughter,” faith and fear (5:33, 36). What Jesus does for the woman shows Jairus what faith looks like just before he needs it.
